At the moment of hatching, a nestling emerges with an initial wet weight of merely 306 grams [Ww0 = 306 grams], a surprisingly modest mass given the enormous size these birds will eventually attain. This relatively small hatchling weight necessitates an extended period of intensive biparental provisioning during the austral summer, when parents alternate foraging trips to sea with brooding duties on the subantarctic breeding grounds. The yolk reserves absorbed during the final days of embryonic development sustain the chick through its first few hours after pipping, after which the transition to exogenous feeding begins once the parents return with a crop full of partially digested myctophid fish and squid. Such a long life, combined with delayed reproduction, shapes a life history in which each breeding event carries considerable weight in terms of individual fitness. These life-history traits are closely tied to the basal metabolic demands of the species.

This high resting metabolic rate is consistent with the pronounced metabolic demands observed in other Sphenisciformes of similar body mass and is thought to be a necessary physiological adaptation for sustaining prolonged diving bouts and extended fasting periods during the breeding season. Comparative studies have shown that this absolute rate, while impressive, scales predictably with the species' large adult body mass, and it provides the energetic foundation upon which all subsequent life-history processes are built. The energetic budget of a breeding adult is particularly constrained during the incubation fast, when males may lose up to a third of their body mass while maintaining this elevated metabolic rate without access to food. Field metabolic measurements taken during the brooding period have further confirmed that oxygen consumption remains elevated even during periods of relative inactivity. Such physiological data are invaluable for constructing accurate bioenergetic models of population-level energy flow through the marine ecosystem.

The energy required to support this growth is immense and is ultimately derived from the marine food web.
